analysis.one_liner: Expands federal workplace safety law to government employees, strengthens whistleblower protections, and raises penalties on unsafe employers.
analysis.headline: The Senate's workplace safety bill, introduced in April 2015 with 4 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strengthen the Occupational Safety and Health Act in three main ways: it would extend federal workplace safety protections to federal, state, and local government employees, who are largely not covered today; it would raise civil fines for violations (for example, from a $70,000 maximum to $120,000 for willful violations, with inflation adjustments going forward); and it would give workers stronger protection from being fired or punished for reporting injuries or unsafe conditions. It would also add rights for injured workers and families of killed workers to follow and participate in the government's investigation of their case.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in dangerous jobs, especially the millions of federal, state, and local government employees who today are largely outside OSHA's coverage. Workers would also gain from higher fines that make violations more expensive for employers, faster correction of serious hazards even while an employer contests a citation, paid time when they help with an inspection, stronger whistleblower remedies (including reinstatement, back pay, damages, and attorney fees), and new rights for injured workers and surviving family members to meet with investigators and be heard before a citation is settled or withdrawn.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers in dangerous jobs, including government employees

how_it_helps.text: Extends OSHA's coverage to federal, state, and local government employees, who are currently largely excluded from federal workplace safety enforcement, and requires states with their own safety plans to conform within 12 months.

Raises civil penalties for the first time: the maximum for willful or repeated violations goes from $70,000 to $120,000, and to as much as $250,000 when a willful or repeated violation caused or contributed to a worker's death; serious violations rise from $7,000 to $12,000; and all penalty amounts adjust for inflation at least every four years.

Strengthens whistleblower protection: retaliation protections now cover reporting injuries or unsafe conditions to the employer or a safety committee, workers who refuse dangerous work in good faith are protected, complaints get an investigation with a decision within 90 days, and prevailing workers can win reinstatement, back pay, compensatory damages, and attorneys' fees; workers cannot be forced to waive these rights by arbitration or contract.

Expands who is protected on a multi-employer worksite: the general duty to keep a workplace free of recognized serious hazards now covers anyone performing work there, not just the employer's own employees, and the employer controlling a site must keep a log of injuries among all workers on site, including contractors.

Adds victims' rights: an injured worker, or the family of a worker who died, can meet with the Secretary of Labor before a citation decision, receive investigation reports at no cost, be notified of employer appeals, and speak before a citation is settled or withdrawn.

Adds new criminal penalties: a knowing violation that causes a worker's death can bring up to 10 years in prison (20 for repeat offenders), a knowing violation causing serious bodily harm up to 5 years, and liability can reach company officers and directors, not just the company.

analysis.who_pays: Employers in hazardous industries — construction, manufacturing, meatpacking, and similar sectors — would bear the cost through higher fines, daily penalties for unfixed serious violations, interest accruing from the day a citation is contested, new criminal exposure for officers and directors, and stricter recordkeeping across contractors. State and local governments, as newly covered employers, would also bear compliance and enforcement costs, and states would have to rewrite their own safety plans to match federal requirements within a year.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hazardous-industry employers and state and local governments

drawbacks.text: The higher fines and daily penalties fall hardest on small, low-margin firms; the bill gives employers with 25 or fewer workers reduced minimum penalties in death cases, but a single willful violation could still cost a small employer tens of thousands of dollars.

The new criminal provisions are broad: up to 10 years in prison for a knowing violation that significantly contributes to a death, 5 years for serious bodily harm, and liability for individual officers and directors, which employers argue exposes managers to prison over contested safety judgments rather than clear-cut misconduct.

Extending OSHA to state and local government workers and requiring states to amend approved plans within 12 months shifts more power to Washington and could strain state safety agencies' budgets and staffing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains for workers are concrete: coverage for currently unprotected government employees, penalties that for the first time adjust for inflation (they had been frozen at levels set decades earlier), and whistleblower rules with real teeth. The costs to employers are real but were calibrated — smaller employers get reduced minimums, and the criminal penalties apply only to knowing violations causing death or serious harm. The strongest objection, on federalism and cost to state programs, was never aired: the bill never received so much as a hearing, so there is no record of the objections being tested or the bill being revised in response.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced and sat there, without a hearing or vote, until that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Al Franken introduced the bill on April 28, 2015, joined by Sen. Patty Murray, who was listed as an original cosponsor in the bill's text.
Four Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions — the standard first step.
That referral was the last action ever taken: the committee held no hearing, reported no bill, and the full Senate never voted on it before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers in hazardous industries are better off, because the higher fines, daily penalties, and criminal exposure never happened. So are the Republican senators who controlled the committee and the Senate, who avoided a recorded vote on workplace safety penalties.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who would have faced higher penalties

sides.party_line_note: Every senator attached to the bill was a Democrat — the sponsor, the original cosponsor, and all 4 additional cosponsors — while none of the Senate's 54 Republicans signed on, and the Republican-chaired committee and Republican-led Senate took no action on it.

industries.industry: Employers in hazardous industries (construction, manufacturing, meatpacking, and similar)
industries.note: The bill would raise fines up to $120,000 per willful violation (to $250,000 where a death occurred), add daily penalties for unfixed serious hazards, extend criminal liability to officers and directors, and require injury logs covering every contractor on a site. Its interest in avoiding these costs runs directly against workers' interest in safer workplaces and real penalties.

industries.industry: State and local governments as employers
industries.note: For the first time, state and local government workplaces would fall under OSHA enforcement, and states would have to rewrite their safety plans within 12 months. As employers, their interest in avoiding federal inspections and fines runs against the government workers the bill would protect.

industries.industry: Staffing agencies and general contractors on multi-employer worksites
industries.note: The bill makes the employer that controls a worksite responsible for logging recordable injuries of all workers on site, including temps and subcontractors, closing a gap these firms have used to keep off each other's injury records.
